displayQuote: Victory is reserved for those who are willing to pay its price

meta.title: Who really said "Victory is reserved for those who are willing to pay its price"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Sun Tzu. The sentence is in no chapter of The Art of War, and no earlier source has ever been produced. Sun Tzu’s actual doctrine is the opposite.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Victory is reserved for those who are willing to pay its price'?
meta.ogDescription: Wikiquote files it as Disputed; it is absent from the text. And Sun Tzu’s real position is that victory should cost as little as possible.

answer.label: Not Sun Tzu — and no earlier source has been found
answer.authorDates: No documented author · apparently a modern saying
answer.sourceLine: This one is not a paraphrase of anything. Search Lionel Giles’s 1910 translation of The Art of War and neither ‘victory is reserved’ nor ‘pay its price’ occurs anywhere in it. Wikiquote files the sentence under Disputed and states plainly that it is not in the text and appears to be a recent creation. No author, no date and no first appearance have been produced by anyone — and the sentiment runs directly against what Sun Tzu actually argues.

source.heading: What Sun Tzu actually argues

docMeta.dd: None located — not in The Art of War

ch. III, v. 2 and ch. II, v. 6

source.excerpt: Hence to fight and conquer in all your battles is not supreme excellence; supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy’s resistance without fighting.
trail: We searched the text rather than the quotation sites. Giles’s 1910 translation is the standard public-domain English Art of War; searched end to end it returns no match for ‘victory is reserved’ and none for ‘pay its price’ the full Giles text ↗

Wikiquote reaches the same finding and files the sentence under Disputed, recording that it is ‘attributed to Sun Tzu in multiple books and internet sites, but this text does not appear in The Art of War and seems to be a more recent creation’ Wikiquote, Sun Tzu — Disputed ↗

What the text does say about the cost of winning points the other way: ‘supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy’s resistance without fighting’ (III.2), and ‘there is no instance of a country having benefited from prolonged warfare’ (II.6) chapters II and III ↗
source.cutTag: Sun Tzŭ, The Art of War III.2, trans. Lionel Giles (1910)
source.excerptNote: This is the heart of the book, and it is the reverse of the quotation on this page. Sun Tzu does not treat the price of victory as a test of will to be embraced; he treats it as waste to be avoided. Chapter II verse 6 puts the same point bluntly: ‘There is no instance of a country having benefited from prolonged warfare.’ A line celebrating willingness to pay victory’s price is not merely absent from The Art of War — it argues against it.

author.name: Sun Tzu
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Sun Tzu
author.metaLine: Traditionally 544–496 BC · Chinese general and strategist · historicity uncertain
author.bio: Sun Tzu is the traditional author of The Art of War, dated by the Han historian Sima Qian to 544–496 BC and said to have served King Helü of Wu. His historical existence is uncertain: the Zuo Zhuan, a detailed chronicle of the period, does not mention him, and the earliest parts of the text probably postdate him by a century or more. Two things make his name a magnet. The text is genuinely aphoristic, so an invented maxim blends in; and it has been marketed for decades as a business-strategy manual, which attracts motivational lines that have nothing to do with it.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: A fabricated quotation usually just fails to be in the source. This one does something rarer: it also contradicts it. That makes the Sun Tzu credit not merely unsupported but actively misleading about what the book says.

items.who: Not in any chapter of the text

context.heading: Why it sounds right anyway
lead: It reads like Sun Tzu because it has the right shape — short, declarative, faintly severe. But the shape is doing all the work. Strip the name off and it is an ordinary motivational sentence about wanting it badly enough, of a kind that has been produced in bulk since long after any Warring States text.

The name is what converts it from a poster into two and a half millennia of tested strategy. That is precisely the trade a fabricated attribution offers, and it is why the absence of a chapter number is worth noticing.
context.detailsSummary: How to check a Sun Tzu quotation in one move
detailsBody: Ask which chapter and verse. The Art of War is thirteen short numbered chapters; a genuine line can always be pointed at.
Search the Giles translation. It is public domain, complete and freely searchable at Project Gutenberg.

Watch for the business-book register. Lines about paying the price, wanting it enough, or outworking rivals belong to modern motivational writing, not to a treatise about not fighting if you can avoid it.
Beware the commentators. Much of what circulates as Sun Tzu is really Tu Mu, Ts’ao Ts’ao or Chang Yu, whose notes Giles prints alongside the text.
context.pull: It is not just missing from The Art of War. It argues against it.
